sources.title: Tyrants, democrats and the first silver ‘owl’ coins of Athens
sources.author: Gillan Davis, Janne Blichert-Toft, Liesel Gentelli & Francis Albarède
sources.scope: Archaic silver sources; chronology of the Laurion discovery; evidence against a simple one-event origin story.

sources.title: Athenian Tetradrachm Coinage of the First Half of the Fourth Century BC

sources.title: When is an owl not an owl? An analysis of Attic tetradrachms circulating in the southern Levant in the late fifth and fourth centuries BCE

sources.scope: Three-quarter-eye owls, contested “Eastern imitation” attributions, the 404 BCE endpoint, and revised Pi-style discussion.
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 70, 105634. Consulted via the author’s full-text copy on ResearchGate. The paper reports 22 sampled coins; the atlas avoids converting a sample-specific argument into a universal authentication rule.

sources.title: The circulation and distribution of classical Greek coinage
sources.author: Zane Mullins
sources.scope: Hoard-based distribution of Classical Greek coinages, including Athenian coins in Egypt, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Iran and Afghanistan, and discussion of foreign imitations.
sources.note: The sample covers 550–300 BCE, not every period or every find. Some older hoard descriptions combine Athens and imitations. Hoard locations do not reconstruct exact trade routes; use, issuing intent and movement mechanisms remain interpretive questions.

sources.title: Hoards and Overstrikes: The Numismatic Evidence
sources.author: Margaret Thompson · Penn Museum, Expedition 21(4)
sources.scope: Published hoard evidence for Athenian coins in Sicily, southwest Anatolia, Egypt, the Levant and farther east; discussion of coins used as bullion.
sources.note: A historical synthesis retained for its documented geographic examples. Its chronology and broad attribution arguments are not automatically adopted; later research, including Gentelli et al. (2026), revisits some eastern imitations. This overview is not a complete gazetteer of finds.

sources.title: Mazaces, Babylon · Le Rider 1997 pseudo-atheniens 10
sources.author: IRIS / University of Oxford
sources.scope: An Athena–owl type attributed to Mazaces and the mint of Babylon, in Babylonia.
sources.note: IRIS gives this type a broad 350–300 BCE range. The geographic introduction uses the mint attribution; it does not extend this date range to every Babylonian owl-type coin or imply an exact issue date. No new specimen photograph is embedded.

sources.title: Greek Art: From Prehistoric to Classical — Coins of Ancient Greece
sources.author: Michael Norris · The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.scope: “Origin and Technique,” printed p. 55 (PDF page 57): hand-engraved dies, a lower obverse die fixed in an anvil, a metal blank and an upper reverse die struck with a hammer.
sources.note: The site uses an original schematic to explain this general method. It does not reproduce the publication’s artwork or reconstruct a particular Athenian workshop, tool set, strike count or coin specimen.

sources.title: Getting started on ancient Greek: 9.1 Athens
sources.author: The Open University · OpenLearn
sources.scope: Ancient Athenian theta letterforms, including the circle with a central dot.
sources.note: Activity 14 compares dotted and crossed theta on Themistocles ostraka. These are examples of Athenian writing, not a catalogue or dating source for the illustrated coin.

sources.title: Erechtheion building accounts, 408/7 BC (IG I³ 476)
sources.author: Translation: Stephen Lambert & Robin Osborne; Attic Inscriptions Online
sources.scope: Wages and piece-rates on the Erechtheion. AIO's note 6 states that the architect and the labourers, both skilled and unskilled, were employed either on a day-wage of 1 dr. or on piece-rates computed on the basis of that wage.
sources.note: Most surviving entries record piece-rates for named tasks rather than counted days; the 1 dr. day-wage is AIO's editorial summary of the accounts, not a quoted line of the stone. The accounts cover one year of finishing work at one building.

sources.title: The First Athenian Owls: Symbols of What, Exactly?
sources.author: Peter van Alfen · American Numismatic Society, Pocket Change
sources.scope: The civic legibility of the owl type and its longevity: the Athenians saw little need to change the basic design until they ceased minting tetradrachms completely in the first century BC.
sources.note: A curator's public-facing post, not a peer-reviewed article. The Peisistratid branding explanation is reported there as a current explanation rather than asserted. The claim concerns the basic type; style and detail changed considerably.

sources.title: Birds 1106–1108
sources.author: Aristophanes; translation Eugene O'Neill, Jr.; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: The bird chorus promises the competition judges that the owls of Laurion will never fail them, that they will move in and nest in the judges' money-bags, and that they will hatch out small change.
sources.note: A comic bribe aimed at the play's judges, not a report of monetary practice. The Greek text is at Perseus text 1999.01.0025, same card; line 1108 reads ἐννεοττεύσουσι κἀκλέψουσι μικρὰ κέρματα. O'Neill's 1938 English may remain in copyright: link and quote briefly rather than reproducing the passage.

sources.title: Silver Tetradrachm, Athens, 515 BCE–482 BCE · 2008.39.34
sources.author: American Numismatic Society
sources.scope: A worn archaic Athenian tetradrachm, 17.047 g, 21 mm, recorded with one chisel cut and a secondary treatment of Cut, from the Asyut hoard (IGCH 1644).
sources.note: The record documents a cut on this specimen. It does not state who made the cut, when or why, and a single record is not evidence for how common test cuts are. Citing it implies no museum endorsement and offers no authentication guidance.

sources.title: The Histories 7.144
sources.author: Herodotus; translation A. D. Godley; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: Revenues from the mines at Laurium; a proposed distribution of ten drachmae a man; Themistocles persuading the Athenians to build two hundred ships instead, for the war with Aegina.
sources.note: Herodotus gives no year, names no coin type, and ties the ships to the Aeginetan war rather than to Salamis. Godley's own footnote calculates that ten drachmae a head would be far too small a sum to build two hundred ships and reads the passage as a contribution to a shipbuilding fund.

sources.title: Athenian Constitution 22.7 (Athenaion Politeia)
sources.author: Aristotle; translation H. Rackham; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: A hundred-talent profit from the newly discovered mines at Maronea; Themistocles has it lent to the hundred richest Athenians; a hundred triremes are built, and with these the Athenians fight the naval battle at Salamis.
sources.note: This account conflicts with Herodotus 7.144 on the mine, the number of ships and the mechanism. Rackham prints the archon's name as Nicomedes; the archon of 483/2 BC is usually printed Nikodemos. The conventional 483/2 BC date comes from the archon year, not from the text.

sources.title: The ANS's Greatest Coins: the first Athenian “Owl”. The dollar of the ancient Greek world
sources.author: Peter van Alfen · American Numismatic Society, Pocket Change
sources.scope: Record of where the phrase “the dollar of the ancient Greek world” actually comes from: the headline of an ANS video post about the first Athenian owl.
sources.note: Held as evidence about the phrasing, not as support for a claim. The analogy is a headline on a video post and is not argued in the body text. Treat it as popular framing attributable to ANS outreach, never as a research finding.

sources.title: Athenian Constitution 62.2 (Athenaion Politeia)
sources.author: Aristotle; translation H. Rackham; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: State pay for public duties: a drachma for an ordinary meeting of the Assembly and a drachma and a half for a sovereign one, half a drachma for the jury-courts, five obols for the Council, and a drachma a day for the archon for Salamis.
sources.note: The Athenaion Politeia describes arrangements of its own time, the later fourth century BC, not a rate fixed for every year. Its authorship is debated; it is transmitted under Aristotle's name. Rackham's 1952 translation may remain in copyright: link rather than reproduce at length.

sources.title: History of the Peloponnesian War 6.31.3
sources.author: Thucydides; translation Richard Crawley; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: The Sicilian expedition of 415 BC: the treasury giving a drachma a day to each seaman, with the trierarchs adding bounties on top of the state's pay.
sources.note: A rate for one expedition that Thucydides presents as exceptionally costly, not a standing naval wage. Perseus publishes this translation under CC BY-SA 3.0 US.

families.name: Archaic
families.feature: A strikingly frontal eye on a profile face; compact, individually engraved forms.
families.detail: The Athena–owl pairing was already established before the classical mass issues. Early style varies: “archaic” is not a synonym for crude. The exact introduction date remains debated.

families.name: Early classical
families.feature: More composed engraving, while the old frontal-eye convention survives.
families.detail: Sometimes called transitional in the fifth-century sense. This label is not the same as the “transitional” owls of the early fourth century. The illustrated museum example is dated 480–449 BCE. Both photographs show the same coin: Cleveland 1920.267, with obverse 1920.267.a and reverse 1920.267.b.

families.name: Classical mass issues
families.feature: Athena, olive, crescent, owl and ΑΘΕ in a familiar, compact design.
families.detail: The mature group dated 440–404 BCE sits within this broader mass-issue phase. The illustrated Met specimen retains its museum catalogue date; the period does not identify a particular year of striking.

families.name: Early 4th-century profile-eye
families.short: A smaller change than it seems
families.feature: Athena’s eye is more plausibly seen from the side; the reverse remains conservative.
families.detail: Frequently cataloged c. 393–355 BCE, with other chronologies using c. 400/390–353. Eye shape is a clue, not a universal dating algorithm: related forms occur in late fifth-century work.

families.name: Pi-style
families.status: Illustrated: Pi III + Pi II · image reuse review pending
families.feature: The developed helmet ornament suggests the Greek letter π; many flans show folding and restriking.
families.detail: The main image is BnF 1966.453.1475, explicitly catalogued as Pi III, c. 353–295 BCE. Pi II, BnF 1966.453.1469, is available in the comparison selector with its broader catalogue date retained: BnF identifies that coin as Pi II and keeps a broad c. 393–295 BCE range on the record, which is not a claim that the Pi II subgroup began in 393 BCE. A subgroup attribution and a catalogue date stay separate. These object dates are distinct from competing wider Pi-style chronologies, including Kroll’s 353 BCE reminting and the early-340s discussion in the 2026 isotope paper.

families.name: Later Old Style
families.status: Illustrated: quadridigité · heterogeneous photo still needed
families.feature: The old Athena–owl design persists in distinct groups, including quadridigité and heterogeneous issues. The illustrated specimen is quadridigité.
families.detail: BnF 1966.453.1478 is explicitly catalogued as quadridigité and dated c. 286–261 BCE in that record; this range is not a date for every later Old Style issue. The heterogeneous issues are a separate third-century group needing their own treatment: CNG’s Electronic Auction 594, lot 66 is catalogued as Heterogeneous Group C citing Nicolet-Pierre and Kroll, Group C, no. 1 as the same dies, not necessarily the same physical coin. That auction specimen is sourced, but its 500 × 240 px preview has not been substituted for a high-resolution reference photograph or for the quadridigité coin above. Reuse review remains pending for the linked BnF photographs.

families.name: New Style
families.short: The owl gets a new world
families.feature: A broader composition: elaborate Athena, owl on an amphora, olive wreath and more inscriptions.
families.detail: The familiar c. 165–42 BCE label is not a universally settled pair of endpoints. This atlas uses a broader envelope rather than assigning every New Style coin one precise terminal date.

families.name: Egyptian owl-type issues
families.feature: Athenian visual language adapted under Persian administration in Egypt.
families.detail: “Attic” can describe a weight convention, not the mint. An owl design or an Egyptian findspot alone does not settle who issued a coin. This named type provides a stronger attribution.

closeReading.note: Markers identify approximate areas, not measured die features.

readings.name: The owl
readings.title: A body in profile. Eyes looking back.
readings.text: The owl’s body turns right while its head faces the viewer.

readings.name: Olive & crescent
readings.title: Small symbols, enduring identity.
readings.text: The olive sprig and crescent accompany the owl on these classical examples. Their presence is observable; a precise commemorative meaning for every detail should not be assumed.

readings.name: The incuse
readings.title: The square belongs to the strike.
readings.text: The reverse sits in a recessed, or incuse, square formed in striking. The minting illustration earlier in the story shows the blow that forms it.

readings.name: ΑΘΕ
readings.title: The city signs its own money.
readings.text: ΑΘΕ abbreviates “of the Athenians.” On this coin theta is a circle with a central dot, the ancient counterpart of the printed Θ, and the form this atlas borrows for its own mark.

readings.name: Athena’s eye
readings.title: The face turns. The eye does not quite follow.
readings.text: The conspicuous almond-shaped eye appears almost frontal although Athena’s face is in profile, a convention already set on the archaic owls of c. 520–510 BCE. In many fourth-century issues the eye follows the face into profile. Eye shapes overlap across the late fifth and early fourth centuries, so this feature alone cannot date a coin.

readings.name: The helmet
readings.title: The detail that names a later family.
readings.text: The classical helmet here is the reference for what changes next. A developed ornament resembling the Greek letter π names the mid–late fourth-century Pi-style family, catalogued on the BnF specimen shown in the atlas.

coda.text: The old Athena–owl design kept going into the third century BCE in several distinct groups, quadridigité among them.

links.label: Compare Pi II with Pi III

steps.label: Athena
steps.title: Athena comes first.
paragraphs: On the obverse, Athena faces right in a crested helmet. Begin with the whole portrait before looking at the engraver’s smaller choices.

steps.label: Athena’s eye
steps.title: The face turns. The eye does not quite follow.
paragraphs: The large almond-shaped eye appears almost frontal within the profile face. Keep it in mind: later owls give Athena a more fully profile eye.

steps.label: The helmet
steps.title: A helmet worth remembering.
paragraphs: The helmet’s ornament is part of the design’s identity. Its later changes help distinguish the Pi-style family you will meet farther down the story.

steps.label: The owl
steps.title: Turn the coin. Meet the owl.
paragraphs: Its body turns right, but its head faces us. The bird stands within a recessed, or incuse, square formed in striking.

steps.label: The olive sprig
steps.title: A branch beside the bird.
paragraphs: An olive sprig fills the space beside the owl. Even on this small surface, the engraver makes room for individual leaves.

steps.label: The crescent
steps.title: A small crescent. An open question.
paragraphs: A crescent accompanies the olive sprig. Its presence is clear; a precise commemorative meaning should not be assumed.

steps.label: ΑΘΕ
steps.title: Three letters. A civic signature.
paragraphs: ΑΘΕ abbreviates “of the Athenians.” The letters are alpha, theta and epsilon. On this coin, theta is a circle with a central dot—the ancient counterpart of the printed Θ.

steps.label: The whole coin
steps.title: All of this, on a piece of money.
paragraphs: A tetradrachm is a four-drachma silver denomination. This specimen weighs 17.2 grams and measures 23 millimetres across: a portrait, a bird and a city’s name on an object small enough to hold.

glossary: The region around Athens in present-day Greece. Athens was the issuing city-state. “Attica, Athens” identifies region and city, not two separate owl varieties.
A weight convention used beyond Athens. The illustrated Cleveland tetradrachm weighs 17.2 g; findspot, weight standard and mint are separate questions.
A denomination of four drachmas. AR in a catalog identifies silver, not a place or a mint mark.
The two faces of a coin. For these Athenian types, the Athena face is conventionally the obverse and the owl face the reverse.
The metal blank that receives the design. Its shape and folded or restruck fabric may preserve evidence of manufacture.
A recessed area. On many older owl reverses, the design lies within an incuse square.
An inscription naming a people or civic community; ΑΘΕ is the abbreviated ethnic of the Athenians.
A stylistic label used two ways: for the refined fifth-century owls and for early-fourth-century issues. A catalogue has to say which transition it means.
A modern stylistic label referring to the helmet ornament—not the value, weight, or mathematical properties of the coin.
A coin using another issuer’s design language. An ancient imitation can be real silver and historically legitimate; this is not the same category as a modern forgery.
A deliberate incision used to investigate metal beneath the surface. A cut is evidence to interpret, not proof of a precise route or an automatic guarantee of authenticity.
A hoard is a deposited group of objects; a findspot records discovery. Neither is automatically the place where a coin was minted.
Circa means approximately. BCE uses the same numbered years as BC: 440 BCE and 440 BC refer to the same year.

places.name: Athens & Attica
places.heading: Begin with a city and its countryside.
places.where: Athens is a city in Attica, the surrounding region on the Greek mainland. Both are in present-day Greece.
places.relation: The starting point: the Aegean world.
places.evidence: Athens issued silver tetradrachms—coins worth four drachmas. Attica also contained the Laurion silver-mining district, introduced in chapter 01.
places.legend: Gold: modern Attica region · dot: Athens city
places.mapNote: The modern region helps locate Attica; its borders are not a reconstruction of the ancient city-state.

places.name: Sicily
places.heading: West, across the sea.
places.where: Sicily is the large island just off the “toe” of Italy. It lies west of Greece, in the central Mediterranean.
places.evidence: Athenian owls occur in Sicilian hoards. These finds document coins reaching the island; they do not make Sicily an Athenian mint.
places.mapNote: Sicily is part of present-day Italy. The highlighted island is a geographic reference, not an ancient political boundary.

places.name: Anatolia
places.heading: Across the Aegean, into Anatolia.
places.where: Anatolia is the large peninsula east of the Aegean Sea, forming the Asian part of present-day Türkiye. Greece faces it across the water.
places.relation: East of Athens, across the Aegean.
places.evidence: Hoard evidence records Athenian coins in southwest Anatolia. That regional evidence does not establish a route through every part of the peninsula.
places.legend: Gold: the Anatolian mainland of modern Türkiye
places.mapNote: The outline is for orientation; the ancient region and its political divisions changed over time.

places.name: Egypt
places.heading: South to the Nile.
places.where: Egypt lies on the southern shore of the Mediterranean. The Nile runs north through it to a broad delta on the coast.
places.relation: South of Athens, across the Mediterranean.
places.evidence: Egyptian hoards include Athenian coins, sometimes valued as silver by weight. Later, authorities in Persian-administered Egypt issued related owl-type coins, including the Sabakes type shown in chapter 05.
places.legend: Gold: modern Egypt · blue: the Nile
places.mapNote: The modern country outline locates Egypt. It is not a map of a particular ancient kingdom or the distribution of coin finds.

places.name: The Levant
places.heading: Along the Mediterranean’s eastern edge.
places.where: The Levant is a regional name for the eastern Mediterranean lands. It includes areas now in Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine and Jordan; its extent varies with context.
places.relation: Southeast of Anatolia; northeast of Egypt.
places.evidence: Athenian coins reached the Levant, and related owl-type issues also circulated there. Some coins once called eastern imitations have been reassessed as Athenian; a findspot alone cannot settle the mint.
places.legend: Hatching: a modern geographic guide to the Levant
places.mapNote: The hatched countries locate the broad region. They do not define a single ancient state or an exact historical boundary.

places.name: Babylonia
places.heading: In the land of the two rivers.
places.where: Babylonia was in southern Mesopotamia, in what is now southern Iraq. The Tigris and Euphrates cross this lowland toward the Persian Gulf. Babylon was a city within it.
places.evidence: Oxford’s IRIS catalogue attributes a Mazaces Athena–owl type to Babylon. This is evidence for a related local coinage, not another name for the Athenian mint.
places.mapNote: The hatched area is an approximate locator, not an ancient border. Blue lines show the Tigris and Euphrates.

places.name: Iran & Afghanistan
places.heading: Farther east than the Mediterranean.
places.where: Iran lies east of Iraq. Afghanistan lies farther east, beyond Iran. These are two distinct countries, far inland from the Aegean starting point.
places.evidence: Hoard evidence places Athenian coins in Iran and Afghanistan. Modern country names help locate the finds; they do not identify who ruled those lands when the coins arrived.
places.legend: Gold: modern Iran and Afghanistan, separately outlined
places.mapNote: The two highlighted country outlines are modern geographic references. No route or exact findspot is implied.

places.name: Arabia
places.heading: A peninsula between two seas.
places.where: The Arabian Peninsula lies between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. Arabia is a wider geographic and historical name, not simply another name for modern Saudi Arabia.
places.relation: Southeast of the Levant; south of Mesopotamia.
places.evidence: Arabian authorities also adopted owl-type designs. This edition marks that wider tradition while leaving a fuller account of Arabian series in the coverage register.
places.legend: Hatching: the countries of the Arabian Peninsula
places.mapNote: Modern outlines orient the peninsula. They are not the boundaries of an ancient Arabian state or a complete record of mint sites.

classical.text: Other classical owls graded NGC Choice XF sold for $976–$1,464 in our seven-coin 2026 sample. Centering, strike and surfaces still differ. This is context for the family, not a valuation of the museum coin.

archaic.text: One archaic VF tetradrachm with a flan flaw sold for $6,710 in January 2026. A single result cannot establish a range for this diverse early family; it does not value the photographed specimen.

early-classical.text: Different early-classical coins sold for $1,464 (Starr IV, Choice VF with scuffs) and $2,928 (Starr V, Choice AU) in 2026. They are different issues and grades, not a price range for the Cleveland specimen.

pi.text: Other Pi-style coins sold for $420 (raw Good VF, worn obverse die) and $793 (NGC MS) including fees in 2026. The sample cannot establish separate values for Pi II or Pi III, or for these BnF specimens.

late-old.text: A quadridigite VF coin with marks and scrapes sold for $570 including fees in July 2026. This is one other specimen, not a valuation of the BnF coin or a price guide to every later Old Style group.

new.text: Other New Style coins sold for $610 (NGC Fine) and $1,464 (Choice XF) in August 2026. Exact issues and condition differ; these examples do not establish magistrate-by-magistrate values or price the museum photographs.
